title: Taurine alleviates dysfunction of cholesterol metabolism under hyperuricemia by inhibiting A2AR-SREBP-2/CREB/HMGCR axis

sections.abstract: Dysfunctional cholesterol metabolism is highly prevalent in patients with hyperuricemia. Both uric acid and cholesterol are independent risk factors for atherosclerosis, contributing to an increased incidence of cardiovascular disease in hyperuricemia. Investigating the pathological mechanisms underlying cholesterol metabolism dysfunction in hyperuricemia is essential. This study identified adenosine and inosine, two major purine metabolites, as key regulators of cholesterol biosynthesis. These metabolites upregulate 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA. Further mechanistic studies revealed that adenosine/inosine up-regulated the expression of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA by activating adenosine A2A receptor via the Srebp-2/Creb axis in hyperuricemia. Additionally, we found that taurine deficiency contributes to cholesterol metabolism dysfunction in hyperuricemia. Taurine administration in hyperuricemia mice significantly reduced cholesterol elevation by inhibiting adenosine A2A receptor. This study provides a promising strategy for treating comorbid hypercholesterolemia and hyperuricemia.
sections.methods:
Taurine was obtained from Beijing Solarbio Science and Technology (Beijing, China). Potassium oxonate (PO) and adenine were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO). Istradefylline was obtained from MedChem Express (Monmouth Junction, NJ). Cholesterol test kit was purchased from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (Nanjing, China). Various purine metabolites (inosine, adenosine, hypoxanthine, xanthine, uric acid) standards were purchased from Shanghai Yuanye Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China, purity >95% by HPLC method). The rabbit anti-Hmgcr antibody was purchased from Thermo Fishier Scientific (Waltham, MA). The rabbit anti-Srebp-2 antibody was purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, MA). The rabbit anti-Creb, anti-Creb phosphorylation ( p -Creb), anti-protein kinase A (Pka), anti-Pka phosphorylation ( p -Pka) and anti-β-actin antibodies were purchased from Cell Signaling Technology (Danvers, MA). The rabbit anti-A2AR antibody was purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (San Diego, CA).

Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were purchased from SPF Biotechnology Co. Ltd. (Beijing, China). The animals were housed in a controlled environment with a 12-h light/dark cycle, a temperature of 22 ± 2°C, and humidity maintained at 60 ± 5%. Water and standard food were provided ad libitum. All animal experimental designs were approved by the Science and Technological Committee and the Animal Use and Care Committee of TJUTCM (No.TCM-LAEC2022006). All mice were acclimatized and fed for 1 week prior to the start of the experiment.

Twenty-five HUA adults and fourteen healthy adults aged 18–60 years were enrolled. Participants were excluded if they had serious health issues such as cardiovascular diseases, respiratory diseases, endocrine diseases, gastroenterological diseases, mental illnesses, or gout. Fasting blood specimens were collected from the participants to measure serum purine metabolites concentrations.

Written informed consent was obtained from all volunteers. The study protocol and informed consent form were approved by Metabolic Diseases Hospital of Tianjin Medical University and Tianjin Medical University (number DXBYYhMEC2017-23-2). The studies in this work abide by the Declaration of Helsinki principles.

The extraction of primary mouse hepatocytes was performed as described previously ( 10 ). Male C57BL/6J mice were anesthetized with isoflurane, and and the portal vein and inferior vena cava were exposed. The liver was perfused via the portal vein with liver perfusion medium at a rate of 5 ml/min until the effluent solution is clear. This was followed by perfusion with liver digest medium at the same rate for an equal duration. The liver was removed and placed in a 15 ml centrifuge tube for digestion. The extracted hepatocytes were filtered through 70 μm cell filters and washed three times with phosphate-buffered saline. The cells were then cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin, and 1% nonessential amino acids in a 5% CO₂ incubator at 37°C. After overnight incubation, the cells were then exposed to adenosine/inosine for another 24 h, with or without istradefylline.

Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were randomly allocated to three groups (n = 7) and were orally gavage the following agents once a day for 3 weeks: 1) control group, mice were administered with control vehicle; 2) HUA group, mice were administered with 200 mg/kg/day PO and 50 mg/kg/day adenine; 3) allopurinol group, mice were administered with allopurinol at a dose of 50 mg/kg/day. To evaluate the effects of taurine, mice in additional groups were orally administered either 200 mg/kg/day or 400 mg/kg/day of taurine in double distilled water once a day.

Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were randomly divided into the control group, adenosine and inosine group (n = 7). The control mice received the 10 ml/kg saline by intraperitoneal injection once a day. The adenosine and inosine group mice were intraperitoneally injected with 40 mg/kg/day adenosine and 20 mg/kg/day inosine for 21 days, respectively. To assess the effect of taurine on A2AR activation, 400 mg/kg/day taurine in double distilled water were orally administrated in this model once a day.

SUA levels were determined by UPLC analysis as described previously ( 11 ). Hepatic cholesterol was extracted using the method outlined in a previous study ( 12 ). The concentrations of cholesterol in both hepatic supernatants and serum were determined using commercial kits, following the manufacturer's protocols.

Serum taurine level was detected by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry as previously described ( 13 ). Serum samples (100 μl) were mixed with 1 ml ice-cold acetonitrile to precipitate protein and kept in ice bath for 30 min. Then, the mixture was centrifuged at 14,000 g for 10 min under 4°C. Supernatant was dried with nitrogen and then re-dissolve with 50 μl acetonitrile and centrifuge at 14,000 g for 10 min under 4°C. The supernatant was used for liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry analysis.

Quantification of taurine was achieved using the Waters UPLC system (Waters Corporation, Milford, MA) coupled to an Exactive™ Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer equipped with an electrospray ionization source (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). The separation was accomplished on a Waters ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column (1.8 μm, 2.1 × 100 mm, Waters Corporation, Milford, MA). The column temperature was 25°C, the flow rate was 0.25 ml/min and the injection volume was 2 μl. The mobile phase A (aqueous phase) is 0.2% formic acid aqueous solution, and the mobile phase B (organic phase) is 0.2% formic acid in methanol. The elution program was as follows: 0–10 min: 60% A isocratic elution.

UPLC analysis was employed to determine the concentration of serum purine metabolites, as previously described with appropriate modifications ( 14 ). The mobile phase A (aqueous phase) is 50 mM phosphate buffer, and the mobile phase B (organic phase) is 0.2% formic acid in methanol. The gradient elution of the mobile phase was shown in supplemental Table S1 .

Cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) was performed as described previously ( 15 ). Primary hepatocytes were treated with media containing 50 μM taurine for 4 h, followed by differential temperature treatment (42–72°C) for 5 min. The heated lysates were centrifuged at 20,000 g for 20 min at 4°C to separate the soluble fractions from precipitates. The supernatants were transferred to new microtubes and analyzed by SDS-PAGE, followed by Western blot analysis using an anti-A2AR antibody.

Drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS) was performed as described previously ( 16 ). Cellular lysates were divided into two parts and incubated with either taurine (50 μM) or dimethyl sulfoxide (equal volume) at room temperature for 20–30 min. Each lysate was then further divided into six aliquots, and proteolysis was carried out with or without varying ratios of pronase E for 30 min at room temperature. The supernatants were transferred to new microtubes and analyzed by SDS-PAGE, followed by Western blot analysis using an anti-A2AR antibody.

The human pRL-TK plasmid, human CRE promoter pGL3-hCRE, and human A2AR expression plasmid were obtained from Genechem (Shanghai, China). HEK293T cells were cotransfected with a reporter construct 250 ng pGL3-hA2AR, 10 ng pRL-TK plasmid, and 500 ng pcDNA-A2AR using Lipofectamine 2000 reagent for 24 h and then treated with taurine for another 24 h. Subsequently, cells were lysed, and the luciferase activities were measured using the Dual-Luciferase reporter assay system (Promega, Madison) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to that of Renilla luciferase activity.

The siSrebp-2 and siCreb were purchased from Hanbio (Shanghai, China), lentivirus-mediated shA2AR vectors were obtained from Genechem (Shanghai, China). The sequences were listed in supplemental Tables S2 and S3 . Primary hepatocytes were cultured to 70–80% confluence and were transfected by using Lipofectamine TM 2000. All the transfections were performed with Lipofectamine TM 2000 reagent according to the manufacturer's instructions. After 24 h transfection, the cells were treated with adenosine/inosine for an additional 24 h.

RNA isolation, cDNA synthesis, and quantitative real-time PCR analysis were performed as described previously ( 12 ). Primer sequences used for quantitative real-time PCR were shown in supplementarl Table S4 .

SPSS 20.0 statistical software (version 20, SPSS; IBM, Armonk, NY) was used to perform statistical analysis. Data was expressed as the mean ± SEM. The Shapiro–Wilk test was used to assess the normal distribution of variables. The independent t test was used to compare the differences between two independent (unrelated) groups. Significant differences between the means of three or more independent groups were evaluated by one-way ANOVA. The least significant difference and Dunnett's test were used for posthoc evaluations, and P < 0.05 was considered to represent a statistically significant difference.
sections.results:
Patients with HUA are often accompanied by elevated serum cholesterol levels ( 5 ). To elucidate the underlying cause of elevated cholesterol in the hyperuricemic state, we established a mouse model of HUA by administering PO and adenine for 3 weeks. Compared to control mice, the SUA and total cholesterol levels were increased by 52.2% ( Fig. 1 A) and 16.5% ( Fig. 1 B), respectively, as well as the content of hepatic cholesterol was increased by 24.2% ( Fig. 1 C) in HUA mice. In the allopurinol-treated group, SUA levels were significantly reduced, while serum cholesterol levels and hepatic cholesterol content remained unchanged compared to the HUA group ( Fig. 1 A–C). D: The mRNA levels of genes involved in hepatic cholesterol catabolism, efflux, biosynthesis, and esterification in mice. E: The protein expression levels of hepatic p -Hmgcr, Hmgcr, Srebp-2(P), m-Srebp-2, p -Creb, Creb, p -Pka, and Pka. Data are presented as the mean ± SEM. ∗ P < 0.05, ∗∗ P < 0.01, ∗∗∗ P < 0.001 versus control group. Hmgcr, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA; ND, not detected; NS, no significance; p -Creb, Creb phosphorylation; Pka, protein kinase A; p -Pka, Pka phosphorylation.

To explore the potential mechanism underlying disturbed cholesterol metabolism in hyperuricemic states, we analyzed key genes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis, catabolism, efflux, and esterification. Compared to control mice, the mRNA and protein expression of hepatic Hmgcr, a rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis ( 17 ) were significantly increased in HUA mice. However, no significant differences were observed in the expression of genes related to cholesterol catabolism (7α-hydroxylase, sterol 12α-hydroxylase), efflux (ATP-binding cassette transporters G5/8, niemann-pick c1-like 1 (Npc1l1), and esterification (acyl-coenzyme A:cholesterol acyltransferases) ( 18 ) ( Fig. 1 D, E). Allopurinol treatment did not significantly affect the expression of genes associated with cholesterol homeostasis. Additionally, the mRNA and protein expression of Srebp-2 maturation (m-rebp-2) and p -Creb, two primary transcription regulators of Hmgcr, were increased in HUA mice ( 19 , 20 ). These findings suggest that upregulation of Hmgcr expression is a key factor contributing to cholesterol dysfunction in HUA.

HUA is characterized by the accumulation of purine metabolites, in addition to the elevation of uric acid levels ( 1 ). As shown in Figure 2 A, purine metabolism regulates the concentrations of intracellular ATP and GTP, which are converted into inosine and guanosine. Purine nucleoside phosphorylase then converts these into hypoxanthine and guanine, respectively. Xanthine oxidase and guanine deaminase further convert them into xanthine, which is oxidized by xanthine oxidase to produce uric acid ( 21 ). We found that serum levels of AMP, inosine 5′-monophosphate (IMP), hypoxanthine, and xanthine were significantly higher in hyperuricemic patients compared to the control group. Similarly, serum concentrations of inosine, IMP, hypoxanthine, and xanthine were elevated in hyperuricemic mice compared to controls ( Fig. 2 C, D), which is consistent with previous studies ( 9 ). However, in the allopurinol-treated group, no significant changes in the concentrations of these purine metabolites were observed compared to the HUA group. We speculated that the elevation of cholesterol in the HUA state is related to the accumulation of purine metabolites. To test this, we first investigated the effect of purine metabolites, including IMP, hypoxanthine, adenosine, xanthine, and inosine, on cholesterol synthesis in primary mouse hepatocytes. The results indicated that adenosine and inosine, but not hypoxanthine and xanthine, significantly upregulated the protein expression of Hmgcr ( Fig. 2 E). Furthermore, treatment with adenosine/inosine significantly elevated the serum cholesterol levels and enhanced the expression of m-Srebp-2, p -Pka, p -Creb, and Hmgcr in primary mouse hepatocytes ( Fig. 3 A, B). E and F: The protein expression levels of hepatic Hmgcr, A2AR, p -Pka, p -Creb, and m-Srebp-2 in mice treated with adenosine and inosine. The protein expression was normalized by β-actin. Data are presented as the mean ± SEM. ∗ P < 0.05, ∗∗ P < 0.01, and ∗∗∗ P < 0.001 versus control group. Next, we investigated the effect of intraperitoneal injection of adenosine/inosine on cholesterol synthesis in mice. Compared to control mice, treatment with 40 mg/kg adenosine and 20 mg/kg inosine markedly increased the serum cholesterol levels and upregulated the expressions of hepatic m-Srebp-2, p -Pka, p -Creb, and Hmgcr. These changes were similar to those observed in the PO and adenine-induced hyperuricemic mice ( Fig. 3 C–F). Collectively, these results indicated that adenosine- and inosine-induced upregulation of HMGCR plays a crucial role in cholesterol dysregulation in the hyperuricemic state.

Adenosine and inosine regulate many physiological processes through adenosine receptors, including A1 receptor (A1R), A2AR, adenosine A2B receptor (A2BR), and adenosine A3 receptor (A3R) ( 22 ). As shown in Figure 4 A, the expression of hepatic A2AR, but not A1R, A2BR and A3R, was significantly increased in HUA mice compared to control mice ( Fig. 4 A, B). Moreover, the upregulation of Srebp-2, p -Creb, and Hmgcr in primary mouse hepatocytes by adenosine and inosine was abolished in the presence of istradefylline, an A2AR inhibitor ( Fig. 4 C, D). A similar effect was observed in A2AR-knock downed cells ( Fig. 4 E–G). These results suggest that A2AR plays a crucial role in the adenosine/inosine-induced upregulation of Hmgcr expression. To investigate whether A2AR regulates Hmgcr expression via Srebp-2 and Creb, two transcriptional activators of Hmgcr, we knocked down Srebp-2 and Creb using siRNA in primary mouse hepatocytes. As shown in Figure 5 A, silencing of Srebp-2 suppressed both the mRNA and protein expression of Hmgcr. Meanwhile, the effect of adenosine/inosine on Hmgcr expression was diminished in Srebp-2–silenced cells ( Fig. 5 A–D), and a similar phenomenon was observed in Creb-silenced cells ( Fig. 5 E–G). However, cosilencing of both Srebp-2 and Creb completely abrogated the adenosine/inosine-induced increase of Hmgcr expression in primary mouse hepatocytes ( Fig. 5 H–J). These results indicate that adenosine/inosine upregulated the expression of Hmgcr by activating A2AR-Srebp-2/CREB axis. Taurine is a nonessential amino acid that plays a crucial role in human metabolism and overall health ( 23 ). To begin, we used liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry to measure serum taurine concentrations in both hyperuricemic patients and mice. Consistent with elevated SUA and cholesterol levels, serum taurine concentrations were found to be lower in both HUA patients and mice than the control groups ( Fig. 6 A). Based on these findings, we explored the effects of taurine supplementation on the cholesterol homeostasis in HUA mice. As shown in Figure 6 B, taurine administration reduced SUA level by 15% compared to the HUA mice. Taurine administration reduced serum concentrations of inosine, IMP, hypoxanthine, and xanthine compared to HUA mice ( Fig. 6 C). Additionally, serum cholesterol levels and hepatic cholesterol content were significantly decreased following taurine treatment ( Fig. 6 D). We then investigated the impact of taurine on cholesterol synthesis and found that taurine administration significantly decreased the mRNA and protein expression of hepatic A2AR, m-Srebp-2, p -Pka, p -Creb, and Hmgcr compared to the HUA group ( Fig. 6 E, F). Furthermore, in the adenosine/inosine-induced mouse models, taurine treatment also led to similar reductions in serum cholesterol levels and expression of genes related to cholesterol synthesis (A2AR, m-Srebp-2(N), p -Pka, p -Creb, and Hmgcr) ( Fig. 6 G–K), mirroring the alterations observed in the HUA mice treated with taurine. We further explored whether taurine treatment regulates adenosine/inosine-induced cholesterol synthesis in primary mouse hepatocytes. Treatment with taurine (25, 50, 100, 200 μmol/l) reduced intracellular cholesterol accumulation and suppressed the expression of A2AR, m-Srebp-2 (N), p -Creb, and Hmgcr, which were induced by adenosine (80 μmol/l) and inosine (200 μmol/l) ( Fig. 7 A–F). To further investigate, we transfected primary mouse hepatocytes with lentivirus to overexpress A2AR. We found that taurine treatment reduced the protein expression of A2AR, as well as the levels of mSrebp-2 (nucleus), p -Pka, p -Creb, and Hmgcr ( Fig. 7 G). Next, we used CETSA, DARTS, and Dual-Luciferase reporter assays to verify whether A2AR is a direct target of taurine ( Fig. 7 H). CETSA results showed that taurine administration significantly reduced the degradation of A2AR with increasing temperature. DARTS analysis revealed that taurine treatment also decreased A2AR degradation with increasing E-streptavidin concentration. Additionally, taurine treatment reduced luciferase expression in HEK293T cells cotransfected with A2AR. Taken together, these biophysical binding assays demonstrate that A2AR is a direct target of taurine. Overall, our results suggest that taurine treatment improves cholesterol metabolism dysfunction in the hyperuricemic state by inhibiting the A2AR-SREBP-2/CREB/HMGCR signaling pathway. sections.discussion:
This study explores the molecular mechanisms in HUA-associated hypercholesterolemia and the regulation effect of taurine on HUA induced cholesterol metabolism disorder. The key findings are as follows: (1) accumulation of adenosine and inosine induces increasing of cholesterol biosynthesis in HUA; (2) purine metabolites, specifically adenosine and inosine, upregulate m-Srebp-2/ p -Creb/Hmgcr axis by A2AR-dependent manner; (3) taurine administration ameliorates dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism induced by HUA by suppressing A2AR-m-Srebp-2/ p -Creb/Hmgcr axis.

It is speculated that uric acid is the trigger of dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism and inducer of cardiovascular disease. Allopurinol, a first-line drug for lowering uric acid, primarily reduces uric acid levels by inhibiting the activity of xanthine oxidase ( 24 ). However, a meta-analysis that reviewed six randomized controlled trials and one before-and-after controlled trial suggests that while allopurinol normalizes uric acid levels, it does not improve serum cholesterol levels ( 25 ). This implies that uric acid may be merely a risk factor for elevated cholesterol, rather than a direct mediator. Furthermore, xanthine oxidase inhibitor treatment did not show any beneficial effect on cholesterol metabolism, suggesting that factors beyond uric acid contribute to cholesterol dysregulation in HUA. HUA is not characterized solely by elevated uric acid, but also by the accumulation of other purine metabolites such as IMP, adenosine, inosine, hypoxanthine, and xanthine. In this study, we investigated the effects and underlying mechanisms of these purine metabolites on cholesterol metabolism dysfunction.

The liver plays a pivotal role in lipid metabolism, with cholesterol metabolism involving processes biosynthesis, efflux, esterification, and catabolism. By screening molecules related to cholesterol metabolism based on mRNA expression variations, we found the expression of the Hmgcr was significantly increased during HUA. In primary mouse hepatocytes treated with adenosine and inosine, the intracellular cholesterol content was notably elevated, accompanied by upregulation of Srebp-2, Creb, and Hmgcr. However, other major purine metabolites did not affect Hmgcr expression. These findings suggest that the dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism in HUA is induced by adenosine and inosine, rather than uric acid itself.

We first confirmed that adenosine and inosine promoted cholesterol synthesis through activation of the m-Srebp-2/ p -Creb/Hmgcr axis in A2AR-dependent manner. Adenosine receptors are G protein–coupled receptors, including A1R, A2AR, A2BR, and A3R ( 26 ). Activation of these receptors alters intracellular cAMP levels by either inhibiting or stimulating adenylate cyclase. A2AR and A2BR activate adenylate cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP levels through Gs signaling, while A1R and A3R inhibit adenylate cyclase, leading to a decrease in cAMP levels through Gi signaling ( 27 ). The cAMP–Pka signaling pathway has been shown to promote Srebp-2 expression, which in turn regulates cholesterol metabolism ( 28 ). In HUA mice, A2AR expression was found to be abnormally elevated, and adenosine/inosine treatment further activated the cAMP–Pka signaling pathway by stimulating A2AR.

Currently, there are three main classes of cholesterol-lowering drugs are commonly used to combat hypercholesterolemia ( 29 ). Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption by suppressing Npc1l1 expression ( 30 ). Statins competitively inhibit Hmgcr expression to reduce intracellular cholesterol synthesis, while also stimulating LDL uptake by upregulating LDL receptor (Ldlr), thereby increasing serum cholesterol clearance ( 29 ). PCSK9 inhibitors block Ldlr degradation, promoting LDL-C clearance ( 31 ). While ezetimibe effectively reduces intestinal cholesterol absorption, no significant changes in Npc1l1 expression have been observed in HUA mice, suggesting that the use of ezetimibe may not benefit hyperuricemic individuals. Statins and PCSK9 inhibitors rely on Ldlr for their cholesterol-lowering effects, which present challenges for patients with defective or deficient Ldlr ( 32 ). Statins, as Hmgcr inhibitors, are widely used in the treatment of hypercholesterolemia and are effective for patients with hypercholesterolemia or atherosclerosis combined with HUA ( 33 ). However, clinical studies have shown that patients with ASCVD-receiving statins still face a higher risk of residual inflammation, which is more strongly associated with future cardiovascular events than residual cholesterol risk ( 34 ). Elevated uric acid is often accompanied by the activation of inflammatory factors to promote atherosclerosis. Thus, targeting LDL-C alone without considering of residual inflammation is difficult to achieve the goal of reducing atherosclerotic risk in HUA patients. Therefore, combining use of aggressive lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory therapy is a necessary therapeutic strategy of care for atherosclerotic disease.

Taurine is a sulfur-containing nonessential amino acid, which has a wide range of physiological effects in regulating cholesterol metabolism disorders. Previous studies have shown that taurine treatment can inhibit the secretion of hepatic very low–density lipoprotein, upregulate Ldlr uptake capacity, and improve periphery cholesterol clearance ( 35 ). Additionally, taurine has been found to reduce the expression of fibroblast growth factor 15 and small heterodimer partner, two downstream target genes of farnesoid X receptor, increase the expression of 7α-hydroxylase, sterol 12α-hydroxylase, and promote the conversion of cholesterol to bile acid ( 36 ). Notably, taurine exerts an Ldlr-independent downregulatory effect on the expression of genes involved in cholesterol synthesis, leading to a reduction in plasma cholesterol levels. Additionally, it is reported that taurine could reduce uric acid levels in HUA rats ( 37 ).

Studies have shown that taurine also possesses some anti-inflammatory effects in vivo. Taurine react with hypochlorous acid to form a more stable compound, taurine chloramine, which can block the production of proinflammatory cytokines ( 38 ). Additionally, taurolidine, a derivative of taurine, has been shown to inhibit the production of TNF-α, thereby reducing the progression of atherosclerosis ( 39 ). Given these properties, taurine could serve as a complementary therapeutic approach for cholesterol-lowering in HUA patients, helping to prevent the onset and progression of atherosclerosis.

In summary, we have identified, for the first time, the mechanism by which adenosine and inosine contribute to dysregulated cholesterol metabolism through activation of the A2AR-Srebp-2/Creb/Hmgcr axis. Additionally, we also found taurine, a safe and naturally occurring compound found in various foods, can ameliorate this dysregulation through the same pathway. This study provides a novel therapeutic strategy for reducing the risk of atherosclerosis in HUA patients.
